items.stem: Kruskal–Wallis is used for:
items.explanation: Kruskal–Wallis is the rank-based omnibus procedure for several independent groups.

items.stem: Friedman is appropriate when:
options: The same units receive several treatments
items.explanation: Friedman preserves the repeated or blocked structure by ranking treatments within each block.

items.stem: For Kruskal–Wallis, observations are:
items.explanation: The pooled ordering is essential because group rank sums compare positions on one common scale.

items.stem: For k groups, the usual chi-square degrees of freedom for either omnibus rank test are:
items.explanation: The common chi-square approximation for Kruskal–Wallis and Friedman uses k−1 degrees of freedom.

items.stem: In Friedman, ranks are assigned:
items.explanation: Each block contributes ranks 1 through k across its k treatments.

items.stem: A significant Kruskal–Wallis result means:
options: Every group differs from every other group
At least one group distribution differs
The largest sample mean is significant
items.explanation: The test is omnibus. A significant result indicates some difference, but does not identify which groups differ.

items.stem: For three groups with n=4 each and pooled rank sums 10, 26 and 42, the Kruskal–Wallis H is approximately:
For k=5 independent groups, the usual chi-square degrees of freedom are:
items.explanation: df=k−1=5−1=4. This is the degrees-of-freedom rule for the omnibus statistic.

items.stem: For N=12 pooled observations, the total of all ranks is:
items.explanation: The pooled ranks sum to N(N+1)/2=12×13/2=78. This is a check on the group rank sums.

items.stem: For four blocks and three treatments, the total of all within-block ranks is:
items.explanation: Each block contributes 1+2+3=6. Across four blocks the total is 4×6=24.

items.stem: For Friedman treatment rank sums 11, 7 and 6 across four blocks and three treatments, Q is:

Which statements about Kruskal–Wallis are correct? A. It is for independent groups. B. It pools observations before ranking. C. Its usual chi-square df is k−1. D. A significant result identifies the differing pair.
items.explanation: A, B and C are correct. D is false because Kruskal–Wallis is an omnibus test; follow-up comparisons are needed.
statements: Its usual chi-square df is k−1.
A significant result identifies the differing pair.

A.why: True: independent samples are the design for Kruskal–Wallis.

B.why: True: a common pooled rank scale is used.

C.why: True: the chi-square approximation uses k−1 degrees of freedom.

D.why: False: it does not identify which pair differs.

items.stem: The Kruskal–Wallis tie correction factor is:
items.explanation: The factor C=1−Σ(t³−t)/(N³−N) adjusts H for tied pooled observations; use the corrected statistic H/C.

items.stem: Which statement describes Friedman correctly?
options: It ranks all observations in one global pool
It ranks treatments within each block
items.explanation: Friedman ranks treatment outcomes within each block, preserving the repeated-measures or matched design.

items.stem: For N=6 with one tied group of size 2 and all other values distinct, the Kruskal–Wallis tie factor C is:
items.explanation: C=1−(2³−2)/(6³−6)=1−6/210=34/35. This is the pooled-data tie correction factor.

items.stem: After a significant omnibus rank test, pairwise differences should be explored using:
options: A paired t test regardless of design
items.explanation: The omnibus statistic only says some difference exists. Follow-up comparisons need a procedure that controls multiplicity.

items.stem: Which statements about Friedman are correct? A. It is for related treatments in blocks. B. Each block contributes ranks 1,…,k. C. Its usual chi-square df is k−1. D. It pools all raw observations globally before ranking.
items.explanation: A, B and C are correct. D is false: Friedman ranks within each block, not in one global pool.
statements: It is for related treatments in blocks.
Its usual chi-square df is k−1.
It pools all raw observations globally before ranking.

A.why: True: blocks preserve the related observations.

B.why: True: every block ranks its k treatment outcomes.

C.why: True: the common chi-square approximation uses k−1 degrees of freedom.

D.why: False: ranks are assigned within each block.

items.stem: For four blocks and three treatments, rank sums are 11, 7 and 6. The Friedman statistic Q is:
items.explanation: Q=12/[4×3×4]×(11²+7²+6²)−48=206/4−48=3.5. The treatment rank sums add to 24.

items.stem: A significant Kruskal–Wallis result can be interpreted as a median difference most directly when:
options: Group distributions have similar shapes and differ mainly in location
items.explanation: The test compares distributions generally. A location or median interpretation requires similarly shaped distributions.

items.stem: Which design should be analysed by Friedman rather than Kruskal–Wallis?
options: Four independent hospitals each use one treatment
Three independent villages provide one sample each
The same 12 participants rate all three products
items.explanation: The same participants rate all products, so observations are related within participant. Friedman preserves this block structure.
